title: Evening with others
hookLine: a shared ritual with family or friends
tomorrow: the guests are gone and you're wide awake. how does an evening end?

cards: Every group chat has one: we should do dinner sometime. Sometime rarely comes. The Talmud tells a Friday-night story that turns sometime into every week.

Rabbi Yose, son of Judah, taught that two angels walk home with a person on the eve of Shabbat, the day of rest: one good angel, and one that is not. They come through the door with you. And they look around the room.

teach.h: THE LAMP LIT, THE TABLE SET.
teach.b: What they look for is plain: the lamp lit, the table set, the bed made.
If they find it, the good angel says, may it be this way next Shabbat too, and the other angel has to answer amen, whether it likes it or not.
If the house is dark and nothing's ready, the other angel makes the same wish, and the good angel has to say amen. That's the whole story, and tradition carries it to the table.

Shabbat is greeted together at a prepared table: candles lit, the table laid, family and guests around it, and in some families a song called Shalom Aleichem, peace be upon you, sung to welcome those angels.
Look at what the angels don't check. Not the size of the room. Not how fancy the food is.
They check whether the house is ready to receive. And look at the blessing: it isn't for tonight.
It's for next week. What you do this Friday tends to become what you do.
The angels are blessing a habit. Shabbat belongs to Jewish life and law, and nobody else needs to claim it.
But anyone can learn what its table teaches about an evening with others: light something, set the table, and let it happen again.

how: Jewish families greet Shabbat on Friday evening with candles, a set table, blessings over wine and bread, and in some homes the song Shalom Aleichem, sung to welcome the angels of the Talmud's story.

o: an evening spent in the same room, each on a phone
a table you set and light for people, week after week
a big party you throw once to impress your friends

games.q: the two angels: tap the pairs.
p: taught the story of the two angels
the lamp, the table, the bed
the blessing is on a habit
the song that welcomes the angels

s: in the story, the angels judge how fancy the dinner is
they look for a lit lamp, a set table and a made bed. Ready, not fancy.
when the house is ready, even the unwilling angel must say amen
the good angel blesses, and the other has to answer amen.
the angels' blessing is for that one Friday night
the wish is 'may it be so next Shabbat too.' the habit is the blessing.

games.q: your family's Sunday dinner has become everyone eating at different times, phones out. what would the two angels notice first?
o: whether the lamp is lit and the table is set for everyone.
whether the food is homemade and fancy enough for guests.
whether everyone showed up in a cheerful mood.
games.why: in Shabbat 119b the angels check the lamp, the table and the bed: whether the house is ready to receive.

practice: Choose one or two people you'd like at your table, a night, one simple dish, and one thing you could light.
Text the invitation now in a single line, or keep it ready to send, and let the breathing hold the picture of the table set and waiting.

wordCard.voice: Evening with others: a shared table, prepared and lit, that comes back week after week, the habit the good angel blesses.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace be upon you, the Friday-night song that welcomes the angels.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: together, at a table set and a lamp lit. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b (Rabbi Yose son of Judah: two ministering angels accompany a person home on Shabbat eve; the lamp lit, the table set, the bed spread; 'may it be so next Shabbat', and the other angel answers amen against its will)
Shalom Aleichem, the Friday-night table song welcoming the ministering angels (living practice, drawn from Shabbat 119b)
